questions.question: Does the patch contain a mosaic of fields with visibly different surface states?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three adjoining field-shaped parcels differ in vegetation redness, exposed-soil color, or texture.

questions.question: Do vegetated fields and exposed-soil fields each occupy a substantial area?
questions.definition: Count yes when field-shaped areas showing vegetation and field-shaped areas showing predominantly exposed soil each cover approximately 10% or more of the patch.

questions.question: Does one uninterrupted field occupy more than one-quarter of the patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when a single field-shaped area exceeds roughly 25% of the image, with no visible internal parcel boundary.

questions.question: Are at least five separate field parcels distinguishable?
questions.definition: Count yes when five or more parcels have boundaries traceable from color changes, vegetation strips, tracks, or other visible separators.

questions.question: Are both small and large fields visible?
questions.definition: Count yes when the largest visible field has at least four times the area of the smallest clearly bounded field.

questions.question: Do fields with straight boundaries occur beside fields with curved boundaries?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least one predominantly straight-sided parcel and one parcel with a substantial curved side are visible.

questions.question: Does exposed ground form a broad continuous surface?
questions.definition: Count yes when one connected, visibly vegetation-poor area of soil or rock covers roughly 10% or more of the patch, excluding roofs and pavement.

questions.question: Is exposed ground distributed among several separate patches?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three soil- or rock-colored areas, each approximately 30 m across, are separated by vegetation or built surfaces.

questions.question: Do wooded areas and low vegetation both occupy substantial space?
questions.definition: Count yes when coarse, crown-textured vegetation and smoother low vegetation each cover approximately 10% or more of the patch.

questions.question: Does a continuous wooded area occupy most of the patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when one connected area with tree-canopy texture covers more than half the image, allowing small internal gaps.

questions.question: Is woodland divided into several separate blocks?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three wooded blocks, each approximately 50 m across, are separated by visibly nonwooded surfaces.

questions.question: Are wooded areas embedded within a predominantly open landscape?
questions.definition: Count yes when open fields or low vegetation cover more than half the patch and contain at least one distinct wooded block.

questions.question: Are open areas embedded within a predominantly wooded landscape?
questions.definition: Count yes when woodland covers more than half the patch and surrounds at least one opening on three or more sides.

questions.question: Do built surfaces and vegetation each occupy substantial space?
questions.definition: Count yes when identifiable roofs or pavement and identifiable vegetation each cover approximately 10% or more of the patch.

questions.question: Is development concentrated in one part of an otherwise open patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when a recognizable building cluster occupies mainly one quadrant while fields or low vegetation dominate the remainder.

questions.question: Does the patch contain several visibly different surface types in close proximity?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three of woodland, low vegetation, exposed ground, built surfaces, and water occur within an approximately 300 m-wide neighborhood.

questions.question: Do two broad surface types meet along a single dominant boundary?
questions.definition: Count yes when two visually distinct surfaces each occupy roughly one-quarter of the patch and share a boundary extending at least halfway across it.

questions.question: Is vegetation interspersed with exposed ground at a finer scale than whole fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when repeated vegetated and bare patches approximately 20–100 m across occur within one larger area rather than only between parcels.

questions.question: Does the patch contain both densely covered and sparsely covered vegetation surfaces?
questions.definition: Count yes when one area has nearly continuous vegetation and another has clearly visible soil between vegetation patches, each spanning approximately 50 m or more.

questions.question: Does a relatively uniform surface contrast with a strongly fragmented part of the patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when one approximately 300 m-wide area is visually uniform while another of similar size contains at least four distinct surface patches.

questions.question: Do several field boundaries share a common orientation?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three separate field boundaries run approximately parallel for visible lengths of at least 100 m.

questions.question: Do neighboring groups of fields have different dominant orientations?
questions.definition: Count yes when two groups of at least three parcels have long axes that differ by approximately 30 degrees or more.

questions.question: Are long, narrow parcels a prominent part of the field pattern?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three visible parcels are roughly four times longer than wide and each is at least approximately 30 m wide.

questions.question: Do several parcels converge toward a common point or narrow corridor?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three field boundaries visibly fan toward the same junction or corridor within the patch.

questions.question: Do visible parcel boundaries form a roughly rectangular grid?
questions.definition: Count yes when repeated approximately perpendicular boundaries define at least four adjoining rectangular or near-rectangular parcels.

questions.question: Does a long linear feature cross most of the patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when a road-like strip, vegetation belt, watercourse, or other distinct line extends at least approximately 800 m within the image.

questions.question: Does a linear feature visibly divide two contrasting landscapes?
questions.definition: Count yes when a traceable line has consistently different surface texture or cover on its two sides for at least approximately 300 m.

questions.question: Do two prominent linear features intersect within the patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when two independently traceable roads, vegetation belts, channels, or comparable features meet or cross inside the image.

questions.question: Does a linear network contain multiple visible branches?
questions.definition: Count yes when a connected road-like, vegetated, or channel-like network contains at least three visible junctions.

questions.question: Does a winding corridor contrast with otherwise straight parcel boundaries?
questions.definition: Count yes when a corridor bends repeatedly across at least approximately 300 m beside fields whose boundaries are predominantly straight.

questions.question: Are there parallel linear features separated by a broad strip of land?
questions.definition: Count yes when two distinct roads, vegetation belts, or channels remain approximately parallel for at least 300 m with 30–200 m between them.

questions.question: Does a narrow vegetation corridor connect two larger vegetated areas?
questions.definition: Count yes when a continuous vegetation strip approximately 10–60 m wide visibly joins two areas each substantially wider than the strip.

questions.question: Is a large vegetated area connected through a visibly narrow bottleneck?
questions.definition: Count yes when two broad parts of one connected vegetated area are joined by a neck less than one-quarter their typical width.

questions.question: Are there isolated vegetation patches surrounded by nonvegetated surfaces?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two vegetation patches approximately 30 m across are enclosed by exposed ground, pavement, buildings, or water.

questions.question: Does a wooded boundary have repeated lobes and indentations?
questions.definition: Count yes when a visible woodland edge contains at least three substantial protrusions or recesses, each approximately 30 m or more deep.

questions.question: Does a wooded area have a long, nearly straight edge?
questions.definition: Count yes when a tree-canopy boundary remains approximately straight for at least 300 m, regardless of its cause.

questions.question: Does an open area have an elongated shape between wooded areas?
questions.definition: Count yes when a nonwooded strip is at least three times longer than wide and has woodland along both long sides.

questions.question: Do several vegetation patches form a visible chain?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least four distinct vegetation patches follow a common line or curve with gaps smaller than approximately twice their typical width.

questions.question: Are surface patches noticeably larger on one side of the image?
questions.definition: Count yes when one half contains mostly broad uninterrupted areas while the opposite half contains parcels or patches typically less than half as wide.

questions.question: Does a surface boundary change from sharp to gradual along its length?
questions.definition: Count yes when the same boundary has one abrupt segment and another segment with a visible transition zone approximately 30 m or more wide.

questions.question: Are there repeated narrow strips along several parcel edges?
questions.definition: Count yes when distinct strips of vegetation or exposed ground follow at least three separate parcel boundaries.

questions.question: Does a broad patch contain a smaller patch with a sharply different appearance?
questions.definition: Count yes when an approximately 30 m-wide or larger area is enclosed by a contrasting surface on all sides.

questions.question: Do visible boundaries form a junction between three contrasting surface types?
questions.definition: Count yes when three distinguishable surfaces meet within an approximately 50 m-wide neighborhood, excluding tiny mixed pixels.

questions.question: Does a corridor widen substantially within the patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when a traceable vegetated, open-ground, built, or water corridor becomes at least twice as wide along its visible course.

questions.question: Does the patch contain both compact and elongated vegetation areas?
questions.definition: Count yes when one distinct vegetation area is roughly as wide as long and another is at least four times longer than wide.

questions.question: Do adjacent fields differ strongly in false-color redness?
questions.definition: Count yes when two neighboring field interiors show an obvious red-intensity or red-saturation contrast in the same false-color image, excluding shadow.

questions.question: Does a single field contain a broad gradient in vegetation appearance?
questions.definition: Count yes when vegetation color changes progressively across at least half a field rather than only at a sharp internal boundary.

questions.question: Does vegetation form irregular patches within an otherwise uniform field?
questions.definition: Count yes when a field contains at least three irregular vegetation patches distinguishable from its surrounding surface in both image context and false color.

questions.question: Does a field contain a broad vegetation-poor interior patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when an area approximately 30 m across inside a vegetated field shows exposed-ground appearance and lacks the surrounding red vegetation response.

questions.question: Is vegetation visibly different along a field margin than in its center?
questions.definition: Count yes when a margin band extends along at least half of one field side and differs consistently from the interior in color or vegetation cover.

questions.question: Are vegetation differences arranged in parallel bands within a field?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three broad parallel bands are resolved within one parcel, excluding display artifacts and single-pixel lines.

questions.question: Does one field contain two sharply separated vegetation states?
questions.definition: Count yes when a continuous field outline encloses two broad areas with contrasting vegetation appearance separated by a clear internal line.

questions.question: Are pale or brown low-vegetation surfaces visible beside green ones?
questions.definition: Count yes when neighboring low-vegetation areas differ from green to pale or brown in true color, with a corresponding difference in false-color vegetation response.

questions.question: Is pale low vegetation accompanied by scattered greener patches?
questions.definition: Count yes when a predominantly pale or brown low-vegetation area contains several greener patches that also show a stronger red response in false color.

questions.question: Do several separate fields share a similar pale surface appearance?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three clearly bounded fields have similar pale or brown interiors, without requiring an inference about harvest or season.

questions.question: Does a pale field contain broad linear patterns consistent with surface working?
questions.definition: Count yes when multiple resolved parallel or turning bands occur within a pale field, without assigning them to a particular agricultural operation.

questions.question: Does vegetation remain conspicuous along boundaries between pale fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when red vegetation strips in false color separate at least two fields whose interiors are predominantly pale or vegetation-poor.

questions.question: Do wooded and low-vegetation areas differ strongly in false-color appearance?
questions.definition: Count yes when adjacent crown-textured and smoother vegetation areas have a clear color or brightness contrast beyond their texture difference.

questions.question: Does a wooded area contain broad zones of contrasting canopy color?
questions.definition: Count yes when one connected wooded area contains at least two approximately 50 m-wide canopy zones with visibly different colors outside obvious shadows.

questions.question: Does canopy appearance change gradually across a wooded area?
questions.definition: Count yes when canopy color or texture varies progressively over approximately 200 m or more rather than changing only at a distinct boundary.

questions.question: Are there sharp internal boundaries within a wooded area?
questions.definition: Count yes when adjacent crown-textured areas have an abrupt color or texture transition extending approximately 100 m or more.

questions.question: Does woodland contain several visible canopy openings?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three openings approximately 30 m across interrupt an otherwise connected tree canopy.

questions.question: Are some canopy openings visibly vegetated?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least one approximately 30 m-wide woodland opening has smoother vegetation texture and a red false-color response rather than exposed-ground appearance.

questions.question: Does tree cover become progressively more scattered toward an open area?
questions.definition: Count yes when a woodland edge passes through an approximately 50 m-wide or broader zone of separated tree groups before reaching open ground.

questions.question: Are tree groups scattered across a low-vegetation surface?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three resolvable crown-textured groups are separated by smoother vegetation within one broad open area.

questions.question: Does vegetation have a repeated row-like texture?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three parallel vegetation bands are individually distinguishable at image resolution, without identifying the crop or tree species.

questions.question: Do repeated vegetation rows contrast with nearby irregular vegetation?
questions.definition: Count yes when a visibly row-patterned area adjoins vegetation lacking a regular spacing or orientation.

questions.question: Is the strongest visible vegetation response concentrated in narrow strips?
questions.definition: Count yes when conspicuously red vegetation in false color occurs mainly in strips less than approximately 60 m wide while broader surrounding surfaces appear less red.

questions.question: Does a broad low-vegetation area appear internally uniform?
questions.definition: Count yes when a low-vegetation area covering approximately 10% or more of the patch has little visible internal variation in either composite.

questions.question: Are broad areas green in true color but noticeably different in false color?
questions.definition: Count yes when two approximately 50 m-wide or larger green areas look similar in true color yet differ clearly in false-color redness.

questions.question: Does a dark true-color surface show a clear vegetation response in false color?
questions.definition: Count yes when an approximately 50 m-wide dark area becomes visibly red in false color, supporting a vegetation interpretation rather than water or pavement.

questions.question: Are yellowish or brownish canopy areas visible beside greener canopy?
questions.definition: Count yes when neighboring crown-textured areas differ clearly from green to yellow or brown in true color, excluding cast shadows and exposed openings.

questions.question: Do canopy-color differences form distinct blocks rather than scattered individual spots?
questions.definition: Count yes when contrasting colors occupy coherent crown-textured blocks approximately 50 m across or larger.

questions.question: Are low-vegetation color changes aligned with parcel boundaries?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three abrupt vegetation-color transitions coincide with clearly visible parcel edges.

questions.question: Does a vegetation-color pattern continue across a parcel boundary?
questions.definition: Count yes when a broad band or gradient can be followed across two adjoining parcels despite their visible boundary.

questions.question: Are buildings arranged along a visible transport corridor?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three resolvable buildings or building groups follow the same road-like corridor for approximately 200 m or more.

questions.question: Does a compact building cluster have a sharp edge against open land?
questions.definition: Count yes when a closely grouped built area meets fields or low vegetation along a clearly traceable edge at least approximately 100 m long.

questions.question: Are separate building groups dispersed through open land?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three identifiable building groups are separated from one another by approximately 50 m or more of predominantly open ground.

questions.question: Does a building cluster surround a substantial vegetated opening?
questions.definition: Count yes when buildings enclose an approximately 50 m-wide or larger vegetation area on at least three sides.

questions.question: Are large roofs visible beside a broad hard-surfaced area?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least one clearly resolved roof approximately 30 m across adjoins a smooth nonvegetated surface consistent with pavement or a yard.

questions.question: Do visibly large and small roof footprints occur in the same patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when identifiable roofs include at least one footprint approximately four times larger than another resolved footprint.

questions.question: Are built blocks separated by substantial vegetation strips?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two building groups are separated by a continuous vegetation band approximately 30 m wide or more.

questions.question: Does vegetation occupy repeated gaps within a built area?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three separate vegetated spaces are resolved among roofs and paved surfaces within one built cluster.

questions.question: Does a road-like feature pass through a wooded area?
questions.definition: Count yes when a continuous linear transport-like surface is visible within tree cover for approximately 200 m or more.

questions.question: Does a road-like feature cross several fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when a traceable transport-like line passes through or between at least three distinguishable field parcels.

questions.question: Does a visible route connect a building cluster to open fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when the same road-like line can be followed from identifiable buildings into an area dominated by fields.

questions.question: Do visible routes form a junction in an open landscape?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three road-like arms meet within an area dominated by fields, low vegetation, or exposed ground.

questions.question: Does a wide transport corridor contrast with narrower local routes?
questions.definition: Count yes when one road-like corridor is visibly at least twice as wide as other resolved routes in the patch, without requiring a road classification.

questions.question: Does development form a narrow extension into open land?
questions.definition: Count yes when a connected strip of buildings projects from a broader built cluster and is bordered by open land on both sides.

questions.question: Are buildings concentrated near a visible route junction?
questions.definition: Count yes when most identifiable buildings lie within approximately 150 m of the same road-like junction.

questions.question: Are rectangular nonvegetated enclosures visible beside buildings?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two sharply bounded rectangular open surfaces adjoin identifiable buildings, without assigning a specific use.

questions.question: Does exposed ground adjoin both buildings and transport access?
questions.definition: Count yes when an approximately 50 m-wide bare area touches a built cluster and a visible access route, without inferring construction activity.

questions.question: Do buildings interrupt an otherwise continuous field pattern?
questions.definition: Count yes when a building group occupies a distinct interruption surrounded on at least three sides by recognizable field parcels.

questions.question: Are visibly regular vegetation blocks associated with buildings?
questions.definition: Count yes when rectangular or row-patterned vegetation areas directly adjoin a building group, without identifying their agricultural or recreational use.

questions.question: Does a built area show a repeated block pattern?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three comparable roof-and-street groupings repeat with a similar orientation and spacing.

questions.question: Does building density change markedly across a built area?
questions.definition: Count yes when one part has closely packed roofs while another has clearly wider vegetation or open-ground gaps between buildings.

questions.question: Does a built cluster contain conspicuously different roof colors?
questions.definition: Count yes when several resolved roofs include at least two clearly contrasting true-color groups, excluding differences caused only by shadow.

questions.question: Does a transport corridor follow a boundary between woodland and open land?
questions.definition: Count yes when a road-like line remains along the woodland–open-land boundary for approximately 200 m or more.

questions.question: Are vegetation belts aligned with visible roads?
questions.definition: Count yes when a continuous vegetation strip follows one or both sides of a road-like feature for approximately 200 m or more.

questions.question: Does a visible route bend around a distinct surface patch?
questions.definition: Count yes when a road-like line follows at least two sides of a wooded, built, water, or other clearly bounded patch.

questions.question: Does a visible water surface have a substantial vegetated margin?
questions.definition: Count yes when a smooth surface identifiable as water from both composites has vegetation along at least half of its visible landward edge.

questions.question: Does visible water form an elongated corridor?
questions.definition: Count yes when an identifiable water surface is at least four times longer than its typical width and is continuously resolved over approximately 100 m.

questions.question: Does a visible water boundary curve or bend substantially?
questions.definition: Count yes when an identifiable shoreline or channel edge changes direction repeatedly over a visible length of approximately 100 m or more.

questions.question: Does a water surface extend beyond the patch boundary?
questions.definition: Count yes when an identifiable water area meets an image edge across a width of approximately 30 m or more.

questions.question: Is open water visible beside fields or low vegetation?
questions.definition: Count yes when identifiable water shares at least approximately 100 m of boundary with recognizable fields or smoother low vegetation.

questions.question: Are wooded areas associated with a visible water margin?
questions.definition: Count yes when crown-textured vegetation borders an identifiable water surface for approximately 100 m or more.

questions.question: Does visible water include a broad area rather than only a narrow line?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least part of an identifiable water surface is approximately 60 m wide or wider.

questions.question: Is a water margin visibly asymmetric in its surrounding cover?
questions.definition: Count yes when opposite sides of an identifiable water body or channel have contrasting cover, such as trees on one side and fields on the other.

questions.question: Do dark nonvegetated patches occur within otherwise lighter exposed ground?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two approximately 30 m-wide dark patches lack a red vegetation response and are not explained by visible cast shadows, without assuming they are wet.

questions.question: Does exposed ground contain a broad dark-to-light gradient?
questions.definition: Count yes when a vegetation-poor soil surface changes progressively in brightness over approximately 100 m or more, excluding obvious illumination gradients.

questions.question: Does a dark ground strip coincide with a band of contrasting vegetation?
questions.definition: Count yes when a dark exposed-ground strip and visibly different neighboring vegetation follow the same course for approximately 100 m, without inferring moisture.

questions.question: Does vegetation form a branching pattern resembling a drainage network?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two narrow vegetation branches join a larger vegetation corridor, with no requirement that flowing water be visible.

questions.question: Does a sinuous vegetation band cross open ground independently of parcel edges?
questions.definition: Count yes when a winding vegetation strip extends approximately 200 m or more and visibly cuts across or diverges from the surrounding field geometry.

questions.question: Are irregular vegetation fingers interspersed with dark open surfaces?
questions.definition: Count yes when several narrow vegetation protrusions alternate with smooth dark nonvegetated areas, excluding identifiable building shadows.

questions.question: Do darker ground patches and stronger vegetation redness occur together within one field?
questions.definition: Count yes when a field contains dark exposed-ground areas beside noticeably redder vegetation patches, without assigning a wetness or drainage cause.

questions.question: Do vegetated field boundaries connect to a wooded block?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two distinct vegetation strips along parcel edges visibly join the same crown-textured woodland area.

questions.question: Does woodland separate two contrasting groups of fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when a wooded strip or block lies between field groups that differ clearly in parcel size, orientation, or vegetation appearance.

questions.question: Are exposed-soil fields concentrated along a woodland edge?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three predominantly exposed-soil parcels touch the same continuous woodland boundary.

questions.question: Do greener-looking fields occur beside a more irregular wooded boundary?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two visibly green fields share boundaries with a woodland edge containing substantial curves or indentations.

questions.question: Does a wooded projection extend into a field mosaic?
questions.definition: Count yes when a narrow extension from a larger wooded block reaches into an area containing at least three distinguishable fields.

questions.question: Does an open field interrupt a wooded corridor?
questions.definition: Count yes when a recognizable field-shaped area separates two aligned wooded segments that otherwise form a visible corridor.

questions.question: Are field-color contrasts stronger than contrasts within individual fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three adjoining fields each appear internally fairly uniform but differ clearly from one another in either composite.

questions.question: Does one unusually patchy field occur among more uniform fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when a field with several broad internal color patches adjoins at least two fields with visibly uniform interiors.

questions.question: Do small fields have more visible vegetated boundaries than nearby large fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when a group of smaller parcels has vegetation along most visible edges while neighboring larger parcels have mostly unbelted edges.

questions.question: Does a route separate fields with contrasting vegetation appearance?
questions.definition: Count yes when fields on opposite sides of a road-like feature consistently differ in vegetation color over approximately 200 m or more.

questions.question: Do field orientations change across a transport corridor?
questions.definition: Count yes when groups of fields on opposite sides of a road-like feature have dominant long-axis orientations differing by approximately 30 degrees or more.

questions.question: Are buildings located where field boundaries converge?
questions.definition: Count yes when an identifiable building group lies within approximately 50 m of a junction involving at least three field-boundary segments.

questions.question: Does a building group sit between woodland and fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when identifiable buildings directly adjoin crown-textured woodland on one side and recognizable agricultural parcels on another.

questions.question: Does a vegetation belt separate buildings from fields?
questions.definition: Count yes when a continuous vegetation strip approximately 20 m wide or more lies between a building cluster and adjoining fields for at least 100 m.

questions.question: Do several routes radiate from a building cluster into open land?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three distinct road-like branches lead outward from the same building group toward fields or other open surfaces.

questions.question: Are fields visibly smaller near a building cluster than farther away?
questions.definition: Count yes when parcels adjoining identifiable buildings are typically less than half as wide as parcels in another visible part of the patch.

questions.question: Does a built area occupy the junction of two contrasting open landscapes?
questions.definition: Count yes when a building cluster lies where two broad open areas differ clearly in parcel geometry, vegetation state, or exposed-ground appearance.

questions.question: Does a vegetation corridor continue through a built area?
questions.definition: Count yes when a traceable vegetation strip enters, crosses, and exits a building cluster without a clearly visible break.

questions.question: Are hard surfaces and exposed soil distinguishable beside the same buildings?
questions.definition: Count yes when a building group adjoins both a smooth pavement-like area and a separate soil-textured area with clearly different visible appearances.

questions.question: Does a broad bare area contain remnants of vegetation?
questions.definition: Count yes when an exposed-ground area approximately 100 m across contains at least three resolvable vegetation islands or strips.

questions.question: Are bare and vegetated strips aligned with the same field geometry?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two exposed-ground strips and two vegetation strips follow a common orientation within one parcel group.

questions.question: Do internal field patterns curve around a vegetation island?
questions.definition: Count yes when visible bands within a field bend around an enclosed tree group or other distinct vegetation patch.

questions.question: Does a continuous vegetation strip have fields of different appearance on its two sides?
questions.definition: Count yes when a vegetation corridor extends at least 200 m between field interiors that differ clearly in color or cover.

questions.question: Does canopy texture differ between a narrow wooded strip and a nearby larger block?
questions.definition: Count yes when a crown-textured strip and a larger wooded area have visibly different coarseness or patchiness at the same displayed scale.

questions.question: Are woodland openings aligned with a visible access route?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least three distinct canopy openings touch or closely follow the same road-like line through woodland.

questions.question: Do sharp woodland divisions align with nearby field boundaries?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least two straight canopy boundaries or internal canopy transitions continue approximately along the orientations of adjoining parcel edges.

questions.question: Does low vegetation form a buffer between woodland and exposed ground?
questions.definition: Count yes when a distinct smoother vegetation band approximately 30 m wide separates tree canopy from a bare surface for at least 100 m.

questions.question: Does a corridor have different vegetation structure on its two sides?
questions.definition: Count yes when a visible road, channel, or open strip has crown-textured vegetation on one side and smoother low vegetation on the other for at least 100 m.

questions.question: Do pale vegetation areas occur in both fields and nonfield openings?
questions.definition: Count yes when pale or brown low vegetation is visible inside a recognizable field and in a separate irregular opening lacking field-like boundaries.

questions.question: Does strong false-color redness occur in both wooded and open vegetation?
questions.definition: Count yes when at least one crown-textured area and one smoother open vegetation area appear conspicuously red relative to other surfaces in the same image.

questions.question: Are vegetation contrasts associated with both parcel boundaries and internal patches?
questions.definition: Count yes when the patch contains clear between-field vegetation differences and at least one field with a separate broad internal vegetation anomaly.

questions.question: Does a regular field pattern transition into an irregular vegetation mosaic?
questions.definition: Count yes when a group of straight-sided parcels directly adjoins an area of interlocking vegetation patches without comparable rectangular organization.

questions.question: Does one linear feature pass through three visibly different landscape settings?
questions.definition: Count yes when the same traceable corridor passes through at least three of fields, woodland, built areas, exposed ground, and water-margin vegetation.

questions.question: Are two visually similar vegetation blocks separated by a contrasting corridor?
questions.definition: Count yes when vegetation areas with similar color and texture lie on opposite sides of a distinct road, bare strip, watercourse, or built strip.

questions.question: Does one part of the patch combine finer parcels, more buildings, and more vegetation edges?
questions.definition: Count yes when one approximately 300 m-wide neighborhood visibly has smaller parcels, more identifiable buildings, and more vegetation boundaries than another neighborhood of similar size.
